rationale: A wins because it finds the sharpest human hook in the update: "On will rent you a running shoe you can never own." That is a real business-model story, not launch confetti. B has useful material, especially "It Has Not Disclosed the Economics," but it keeps inflating questions into theses and wanders into unsupported filler like "Consumer mail-back programs in other categories have historically struggled with low return rates." A is tighter, cleaner, and more pitchable.
gaps_in_A: "runners track shoe mileage obsessively" is plausible, but it is not in the update; the runner angle should mark that as a reporting hypothesis, not a fact.
"this model hands the retirement decision to the brand" overstates what is known. The update says subscribers mail the shoe back; it does not say who decides when.
The castor-bean angle needs more caution around "a demand signal for an agricultural supply chain" because no volume, sourcing, or production forecast is disclosed.
gaps_in_B: "Consumer mail-back programs in other categories have historically struggled with low return rates" is invented outside evidence. You do not get to smuggle in a trend without sourcing it.
"investors and analysts are being asked to accept the model on faith" overplays the finance angle. The update gives no evidence the subscription is material to On's business.
"A circular economy reporter at a sustainability trade outlet or a business journalist" is too broad compared with a real sub-beat; it reads like targeting by directory category.
The category angle and return-behavior angle both orbit the same missing proof: return rate and viability. They are related enough that B needs a sharper separation or one should be cut.
